summary: Updates the H ratio from RFC 1715 and defines a new ratio, which the authors say is easier to understand, for measuring how efficiently addresses are assigned.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3194 introduces a way to say how full an addressing plan is. It divides the logarithm of the number of addresses in use by the logarithm of the number the plan could hold, and gives the result as a percentage. Networks that had to renumber when they could bear it no longer all sat at the same point on the older measure, but they all sat around 87% on this one.

subtitle: A single percentage that says how full an address space is, and how soon the operator will have to renumber

tldr.problem: An addressing plan wastes part of its space at every level of its hierarchy, and the losses multiply, so a simple count of used addresses does not say when an operator will be forced to renumber.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the Host Density ratio as the logarithm of the number of allocated objects divided by the logarithm of the number the plan could hold, and shows it can be read as a percentage between 0 and 100.
tldr.outcome: Three networks that renumbered when they could bear it any longer all sat between 86.7% and 87.5% on the new measure, while values of 80% or less were comfortable, so the ratio becomes a practical warning that an address plan is close to full.

facts.label: HD-ratio range
facts.value: 0 to 1, usually shown as a percentage

today: RFC 3194 is an Informational memo from November 2001 that updates RFC 1715 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It offers the HD-ratio as a proposed replacement for the H-Ratio, for operators who need to judge how much room an address plan has left.

sections.title: Why Address Efficiency Needs a Measure
sections.content:
A naive observer might assume that the number of addressable objects in an addressing plan is a linear function of the size of the address. If that were true, a telephone numbering plan based on 10 digits could number 10 billion telephones, and the IPv4 32-bit addresses would be adequate for numbering 4 billion computers. It is not true: the 10-digit plan is stressed today and handles only a few hundred million telephones in North America, and the Internet registries started implementing increasingly restrictive allocation policies when there were only a few tens of million computers on the Internet.

Addressing plans are organised as a hierarchy. In telephony the first digits designate a region, the next digits an exchange, and the last digits a subscriber within that exchange. In computer networks the most significant bits designate an address range allocated to a network provider, the next bits the network of an organisation served by that provider, and then the subnet the individual computers are connected to. Each level needs some margin, because the number of elements at that level changes over time through growth and mobility. If the current allocation is exceeded, renumbering follows, which is painful and expensive. Squeezing too many objects into a hierarchical address space increases the pain.

The IPNG debates of 1993 asked what ratio of utilisation was acceptable, because such a ratio says how many computers could be connected and helps size the next generation of addresses. The second question has been answered, with 128-bit addresses for IPv6, but the first is still relevant: knowing the capacity of the current plan helps predict the date when that capacity will be exceeded. The earliest attempt at a ratio divided the number of allocated addresses by the size of the address space. That measure depends heavily on the size of the space, and it misses the fact that the loss of efficiency at each level of a hierarchy has a multiplicative effect: 50% efficiency at each stage of a three-level hierarchy results in an overall efficiency of 12.5%. A pain indicator therefore needs a ratio that accounts for those multiplicative effects. The H-Ratio defined in RFC 1715 did this, as the base 10 logarithm of the number of allocated addresses divided by the size of the address in bits. It is independent of address size, but its values run only from 0.0 to 0.30103, typically 0.20 to 0.28, and experience has shown that those numbers are difficult to explain to other people.
sections.plainLanguage: Address space is wasted at every level of its hierarchy, and the losses multiply: three levels at 50% each leave only 12.5% usable. A useful measure has to account for that, and the older H-Ratio did but produced numbers nobody could explain. This memo replaces it with a percentage.

sections.title: The HD-Ratio Formula
sections.content:
When considering an addressing plan that allocates objects, the host density ratio HD is defined as the logarithm of the number of allocated objects divided by the logarithm of the maximum number of allocatable objects. The ratio is defined for any maximum number of allocatable objects greater than 1, and any number of allocated objects greater than or equal to 1 and less than or equal to that maximum.

The ratio is usually presented as a percentage, for example 70%. It varies between 0, when there is just one allocation, and 1, when there is one object allocated to each available address. Any base can be used for the logarithm, as long as the same base is used for the numerator and the denominator. In most cases the HD-ratio can be derived from the H ratio by the formula HD = H divided by log10(2).
sections.plainLanguage: Divide the logarithm of how many objects are allocated by the logarithm of how many could be. The result is a number between 0 and 1, which is easier to read as a percentage. It can also be worked out from the older H ratio.

sections.title: Reading the HD-Ratio as a Pain Level
sections.content:
To test whether the ratio predicts the pain caused by a given efficiency, the earlier memo used several examples of networks that had reached their capacity limit. These were telephone networks at the point where they decided to add a digit to their numbering plan, and computer networks at the point where their addressing capability was perceived as stretched beyond practical limits. The reasoning was that network managers delay renumbering or changing the network protocol until it becomes too painful, so the ratio just before the change is a good predictor of what can be achieved in practice.

The first example was the French telephone network, which added one digit to all numbers, moving from 8 digits to 9, when the number of phones reached a threshold of 1.0E+7. That is an HD-ratio of 87.5% before the change and 77.8% after it. The second was the US telephone system, which expanded the number of areas, making the phone number effectively 10 digits long instead of 9.2, for about 1.0E+8 subscribers: 87.0% before the change and 80.0% after it. The third was DECnet Phase IV, the globally connected physics and space science network, which stopped growing at about 15K nodes, with new nodes hidden, in a 16-bit address space: 86.7%.

These addressing systems reached their limits at very close values of the HD-ratio. In the same three examples the direct quotients were 10%, 3.2% and 22.8%, three very different numbers that lead to no obvious generalisation, while the HD-ratio puts all three close together. The examples suggest that an HD-ratio value on the order of 85% and above corresponds to a high pain level, at which point operators are ready to make drastic decisions. Looking at the same examples the other way, the operators who renumbered tried to reach a pain level that was easily supported afterwards: the HD-ratio of the French and US networks immediately after renumbering was 78% and 80% respectively, which suggests that values of 80% or less correspond to comfortable trade-offs between pain and efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo checks the measure against three networks that changed when they could bear it no longer. All three were between 86.7% and 87.5% full on the new measure, while the old measure gave them three unrelated answers. A reading of 85% or more means operators are close to making a drastic change.

sections.title: How Many Objects an Address Plan Can Hold
sections.content:
Using the HD-ratio directly makes it easy to evaluate the density of allocated objects. Evaluating how well an addressing plan will scale requires the reverse calculation. Because an HD-ratio lower than 80% is manageable and ratios higher than 87% are hard to sustain, the acceptable and practical maximum number of objects that can be allocated for a given address size can be computed as the maximum number of allocatable objects raised to the power of the HD-ratio.

The memo gives example values for a 9-digit telephone plan, a 10-digit telephone plan and the 32-bit IPv4 Internet. For a 9-digit plan the numbers run from 16M at 80% to 68M at 87%. For a 10-digit plan they run from 100M to 500M. For 32-bit addresses they run from 51M at 80%, through 154M at 85% and 192M at 86%, to 240M as the practical maximum at 87%. One M is 1,000,000. The practical maximum depends on the level of pain that users and providers are willing to accept, and the authors note that more than 154M allocated IPv4 addresses may well be reached in the next years if that pain is accepted.
sections.plainLanguage: The measure works backwards too: raise the size of the address space to the power of the HD-ratio and you get the number of objects that fit. For IPv4 that is 51 million at 80% and 240 million at the practical limit of 87%.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The memo states that the document has no security implications. It also states that it does not request any IANA action, since the HD-ratio is a way of measuring rather than a protocol or a registry.

The references give the sources behind the numbers: the H Ratio for Address Assignment Efficiency in RFC 1715, the IANA registry of the Internet Protocol version 4 address space, the Internet Domain Survey maintained by the Internet Software Consortium, and Netsizer from Telcordia Technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo only measures something, so it changes nothing on the network and asks the IANA for nothing. It measures how full an address plan is.
